name: Republic of Texas
info: A short-lived slaveholding republic carved from Mexico by Anglo-American settlers in 1836, at war with Mexico and the Comanches until its annexation by the United States in 1845.

facts.capital: Washington-on-the-Brazos, Harrisburg, Galveston, Velasco and Columbia (1836), Houston (1837), Austin (1839)
facts.founder: The delegates of the Convention of 1836; David G. Burnet interim president, Sam Houston the first elected president
facts.predecessor: Mexican Texas, part of the state of Coahuila y Tejas in the Mexican republic
facts.successor: The State of Texas, the 28th state of the United States (annexed 29 December 1845)

t: Texas declared independence from Mexico on 2 March 1836, after Santa Anna's Siete Leyes centralised the Mexican republic and he began enforcing laws against slavery, which Mexico had abolished in 1829 and which the Texians refused to end.

Its 1836 constitution made slavery a cornerstone of the state: slaves could not be freed without the consent of Congress, Congress could pass no law against slavery or the slave trade, and no free person of African descent could reside permanently in the republic.
Only seven nations recognised Texas, and its claim to the Rio Grande as its border, disputed by Mexico throughout, passed to the United States at annexation and led to the Mexican–American War.
dyk: In 1839 Texas became the first nation in the world to enact a homestead exemption, under which creditors cannot seize a person's primary residence.
ev: On 2 October hostilities between Texian settlers and Mexican troops open at the Battle of Gonzales, the first engagement of the Texas Revolution.
On 2 March the Convention of 1836 proclaims the Texas Declaration of Independence; David G. Burnet becomes interim president.
On 21 April major fighting ends, and the Treaties of Velasco, signed by Santa Anna as a prisoner, secure Texas's independence, which the Mexican Congress refuses to recognise.
On 3 March President Andrew Jackson appoints Alcée La Branche chargé d'affaires, the United States officially recognising the republic.
President Mirabeau B. Lamar moves the capital to the new town of Austin; the Lone Star Flag is adopted and France recognises Texas on 25 September.
After 34 Comanche leaders are massacred at peace talks in San Antonio, Buffalo Hump leads the Great Raid of 1840 to the Gulf coast; the Comanches are caught at the Battle of Plum Creek.
On 11 September Adrián Woll's 1,400 Mexican troops capture San Antonio; Texans fight at the Battle of Salado Creek while 53 surrendered volunteers are massacred nearby.
On 29 December Texas is annexed and admitted as the 28th state of the United States; power passes from the republic on 19 February 1846.

sections.foundation:
Texas had been a thinly settled province of Spain, where Anglo-American filibusters proclaimed short-lived republics in 1813 and 1819. After Mexican independence in 1821 Stephen F. Austin led the Old Three Hundred into the province and other empresarios followed; in 1824 Texas was joined with Coahuila as the state of Coahuila y Tejas. High cotton prices and the success of the Mississippi plantations drew large numbers of white Americans with slaves to copy that model. Mexico abolished slavery in 1829, but the Texians refused to end it, replacing it with long-term indenture contracts signed by "liberated" slaves, and the Law of April 6, 1830 outlawed American immigration. The empresarios' Convention of 1832 was the first formal step towards revolution.

By 1834 American immigrants greatly outnumbered Mexicans. When Antonio López de Santa Anna's regime adopted the Siete Leyes, abolishing the authority of the states, and began enforcing the anti-slavery laws, the settlers objected to mandatory Catholicism and feared worse. In 1835 the central government split Coahuila y Tejas in two; fighting opened at the Battle of Gonzales on October 2, 1835, and a provisional government, the Consultation, formed in November. The Convention of 1836 met on March 1 and declared independence the next day. David G. Burnet became interim president with Lorenzo de Zavala as vice-president; major fighting ended on April 21, 1836, and Sam Houston was elected president on September 5.
sections.socioeconomy:
The republic's economy rested on farming and on slavery, a cornerstone of the Texian economy, above all in agriculture. Its main exports were crops, chiefly cotton and corn; it imported iron, machinery and goods such as tea, beer and chocolate from the nations that recognised it, and small amounts went to Russia and Spain. Settlers from the southern states brought slavery with them; it fuelled the economy and reinforced social inequality. The Constitution of 1836 wrote it into law: African slaves brought to Texas remained slaves and could not be emancipated without the consent of Congress, Congress could make no law restricting slavery or the slave trade, and no free person of African descent, in whole or in part, might reside permanently in the republic without that consent. Texans of Mexican descent were Tejanos, the Anglo-Americans Texians; women worked in domestic labour, agriculture and business with very limited legal rights.

Public finance was weak: there was no central bank, the Texas dollar was volatile and private banking largely unregulated. The cotton price crash of the 1840s bankrupted the republic, and its government's huge debts became a motive for annexation. Congress nevertheless chartered colleges, from the University of San Augustine in 1837 to Baylor University in 1845. In 1839 Texas became the first nation to enact a homestead exemption protecting a person's primary residence from creditors.
sections.military:
The republic was never at peace. The Comanches, whose territory included north-west Texas, were its main Indigenous opponents. Sam Houston negotiated peace with them in the late 1830s, but Mirabeau B. Lamar reversed that policy in 1838 and ordered an invasion of Comancheria. After peace talks in 1840 ended with the massacre of 34 Comanche leaders in San Antonio, Potsanaquahip (Buffalo Hump) led 500 to 700 Comanche cavalry down the Guadalupe valley to the Gulf of Mexico, sacking Victoria and Linnville in the Great Raid of 1840; pursued by 186 rangers, they lost their plunder at the Battle of Plum Creek. Houston, president again in 1841, made a new peace with both sides exhausted; the Treaty of Tehuacana Creek of 1844, signed without the Comanches, could not be enforced for want of men and money.

Mexico refused to recognise independence. Lamar's unofficial Santa Fe Expedition of 1841, 320 soldiers with merchants, aimed at eastern New Mexico; its members were captured, and two raids on the Santa Fe Trail in 1843 also failed. On March 5, 1842 Ráfael Vásquez's 500 men briefly occupied San Antonio, and on September 11 Adrián Woll's 1,400 captured it; Texans fought them at the Battle of Salado Creek while, a mile and a half away, Mexican soldiers massacred 53 volunteers who had surrendered. At sea the Texas Navy's Austin and Wharton under Commodore Edwin Ward Moore fought the Mexican steamers inconclusively at the Naval Battle of Campeche in 1843 beside Yucatán.
sections.governance:
The Constitution of 1836 made Texas a centralised unitary state, unlike the federal United States. In September 1836 the republic elected a Congress of 14 senators and 29 representatives; the first president served two years, later ones three, and only male citizens could vote or hold office. A Supreme Court had a chief justice appointed by the president, James Collinsworth the first, and four associates elected by both houses for four-year terms, who also presided over four judicial districts; each of the 23 counties had its own court, sheriff, coroner and justices of the peace. Five sites served as capitals in 1836 before Houston in 1837 and, under Lamar in 1839, the new town of Austin, confirmed as the seat of government by the Archive War, when the archives Houston had removed were returned at gunpoint.

Citizenship followed race. Section 10 made all residents on the day of independence citizens except "Africans, the descendants of Africans, and Indians"; white immigrants qualified after six months and an oath of loyalty. Politics turned on two factions: the War Party under Lamar, for independence, the expulsion of the Native Americans and expansion to the Pacific, and the Peace Party under Houston, for annexation and coexistence. Congress even claimed The Californias over Houston's veto. The 1844 election split the republic, the newer western regions for Edward Burleson and the cotton country east of the Trinity River for Anson Jones.
sections.impact:
Texas's status as a slaveholding country and Mexico's claim on its territory shaped all its foreign relations. Only seven nations recognised it: the United States on March 3, 1837, when Andrew Jackson appointed Alcée La Branche chargé d'affaires; France on September 25, 1839, whose Legation of 1841 still stands in Austin; Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, which exchanged recognition for free trade, the Republic of Yucatán, and the United Kingdom, which admitted Texian goods while deferring to Mexico and recognised the republic in the 1840s, after the cotton crash, in a failed attempt to coerce it into giving up slavery and to check American expansion.

Though most Texians wanted annexation from the start, both Democrats and Whigs in Washington resisted adding a vast slaveholding region to a country already divided over slavery, and feared war with Mexico. The republic's claims outran its reach: it took the Rio Grande as its boundary, including eastern New Mexico, which Mexico administered throughout, and hoped for a railroad to the Gulf of California; much of the disputed land was Comanche country outside either state's control, and some districts sent representatives to both congresses. Those claims, inherited by the United States, led to the Mexican–American War. The Naval Battle of Campeche is engraved on the cylinder of every Colt 1851 Navy, 1860 Army and 1861 Navy revolver.
sections.decline:
The cotton price crash of the 1840s bankrupted the republic and made foreign protection against a Mexican reconquest urgent, while its debts argued for annexation. On February 28, 1845 the U.S. Congress passed a bill authorising it, which President John Tyler signed on March 1, with the date set for December 29. The British and French ministers hurried to Mexico City, where Mexico signed a "Diplomatic Act" offering to recognise an independent Texas with mediated boundaries. President Anson Jones sent both offers to a specially elected convention at Austin, which accepted the American proposal with one dissenting vote; the Mexican offer was never put to a vote.

On October 13, 1845 a large majority of voters approved annexation and a state constitution that specifically endorsed slavery and the bringing of slaves into Texas. Congress accepted it, and Texas became a state on December 29, 1845, bypassing any territorial phase; the republic formally handed over power on February 19, 1846. The joint resolution allowed up to four more states to be made from its territory and let Texas keep its public lands, so that the state later controlled its oil reserves. In the Compromise of 1850 Texas sold its claims beyond its present borders for $10,000,000 in federal bonds. The border dispute with Mexico, which had refused to sell or to recognise, passed to Washington and brought on the Mexican–American War.

summary: The Republic of Texas, declared by Anglo-American settlers on 2 March 1836 after Santa Anna centralised Mexico and moved against slavery, wrote slavery and white citizenship into its constitution, fought Mexico and the Comanches for nine years, won recognition from seven nations and, bankrupt after the cotton crash, joined the United States on 29 December 1845.

Paul D. Lack, The Texas Revolutionary Experience: A Political and Social History 1835–1836 (Texas A&M University Press, 1992)

pointDescs.1836: Independence is declared on March 2; fighting ends on April 21 with the Treaties of Velasco, and Sam Houston is elected president in September while Mexico refuses to recognise the republic.
pointDescs.1837: The United States recognises Texas on March 3; the capital moves to Houston and the first college is chartered.
pointDescs.1838: Mirabeau B. Lamar becomes president, reverses Houston's peace with the Comanches and orders the invasion of Comancheria.
pointDescs.1839: The republic's high point: Austin becomes the capital, the Lone Star Flag is adopted, France grants recognition and Texas enacts the world's first homestead exemption.
pointDescs.1840: The massacre of 34 Comanche leaders in San Antonio brings the Great Raid of 1840 to Victoria and Linnville; the rangers recover the plunder at Plum Creek.
pointDescs.1841: Houston returns as president and makes peace with the exhausted Comanches; the Santa Fe Expedition ends in capture, and the cotton crash begins to bankrupt the state.
pointDescs.1842: Mexican forces under Vásquez and Woll occupy San Antonio twice; 53 surrendered volunteers are massacred near Salado Creek and the Mier raid fails.
pointDescs.1843: The Texas Navy fights the Mexican steamers at Campeche beside Yucatán; two raids on the Santa Fe Trail fail.
pointDescs.1844: The Treaty of Tehuacana Creek is signed without the Comanches and cannot be enforced; the election divides west from cotton country and Anson Jones wins.
pointDescs.1845: Bankrupt and in debt, Texas votes on October 13 for annexation and a constitution endorsing slavery, and becomes the 28th state on December 29.

notes: The register ends the republic in 1845 (annexation on December 29, 1845); the article's own end date is February 19, 1846, when power was formally transferred: the last point is 1845 as the register requires and the 1846 transfer is mentioned in the text.
The article does not name the 53 massacred volunteers' commander, so the text speaks only of 53 surrendered volunteers.
Points use calendar years only, so the Declaration (March), the Treaties of Velasco (April) and Houston's election (September) share the 1836 point.
'Massacre of 34 Comanche leaders in San Antonio' is the article's wording; it does not use the name Council House Fight.
Left out for space: the Regulator–Moderator War (1839–1844), the Spanish-era republics of 1813 and 1819 in detail, Guadalupe College and the Herman University charters.
References are from the article's Citations and Further reading lists.
